title: NLP & linguistics — where it stands
eyebrow: Capability positioning · read from the source, not from memory
thesis: A deterministic, fully-embedded classic NLP pipeline — UAX#29 tokenization, 25-language Snowball stemming, an averaged-perceptron POS tagger (NLTK's own model, reimplemented in Zig), VADER sentiment, RAKE + TextRank + TF-IDF keywords, WordNet, phonetics — with zero downloads and a one-line first contact. Its own stated target is to beat NLTK on simplicity, and against NLTK it largely does. But it sits a full tier below spaCy and Stanza: NER is gazetteer-rule not neural, there is no dependency parsing, and the neural upgrades (transformer NER, embeddings, abstractive summary) are wired but no-op without a local model — gated on the still-unstarted ggml/GGUF foundry.
grid_title: Twelve lanes, each against its category leader
grid_lede: Every lane names what actually ships, the tools it is fair to measure against, and the one thing still owed. The axis that matters here is deterministic/dictionary vs neural: this tier is the former by design, with the latter deferred to a local-model upgrade.

lanes.engine: `word_break.zig` implements the full UAX#29 word-boundary state machine — `WordIter` / `SentenceIter` are the shared seam every lane routes through. Sentence splitting handles terminator runs, ellipses, abbreviations (`Dr.`) and in-token dots (`example.com`).
lanes.owed: CJK and Thai break per-codepoint pending true dictionary segmentation (libthai/ICU is the named future step) — the one deviation from full correctness.

lanes.engine: Vendored Snowball (`stem.zig`) across 25 languages — english, arabic, french, german, russian, hindi, tamil, turkish and more — the reference algorithm, engine-backed, with per-language and auto-detect entry points.
lanes.owed: At reference parity — it is Snowball. spaCy doesn't stem at all; this is a lane where the classic approach is simply the right one.

lanes.engine: All three classic methods, engine-backed: RAKE (`textutil.zig`), TextRank keywords + extractive summary (`textrank.zig`, PageRank over a co-occurrence graph), and TF-IDF keywords (`textstats.zig`, with corpus-level IDF via `stzCorpus`).
lanes.owed: Having RAKE, TextRank and TF-IDF plus extractive summarization in one engine is broader than most single libraries offer. A genuinely strong lane.

lanes.engine: `pos.zig` — an averaged perceptron, a faithful reimplementation of NLTK's `averaged_perceptron_tagger` (Penn Treebank), with the trained weights (~75k features) `@embedFile`'d and deterministic argmax. No ML runtime.
lanes.owed: English only, and a trained linear model sits below spaCy/Stanza's neural taggers on accuracy. At NLTK parity because it is NLTK's model.

lanes.engine: `sentiment.zig` — a faithful VADER (Hutto & Gilbert): a 7,500-term lexicon plus the five rule heuristics (caps emphasis, degree boosters with distance damping, negation, contrastive "but", punctuation), with an explainable breakdown.
lanes.owed: English only and rule-based — below a fine-tuned transformer on nuanced text. Faithful to VADER, which is the point; the neural upgrade is deferred.

lanes.engine: `lemma.zig` — dictionary form→lemma lookup for en / fr / ar (the fr table is 4.5 MB), plus an English regular-suffix rule fallback validated against the lemma set. Irregulars (mice→mouse) covered by the tables.
lanes.owed: POS-blind and three languages. Ambiguous forms resolve by an alphabetical tie-break (`better→well`) — pinned by a test as an artifact, not a policy. POS-aware lemmatization is the accuracy step.

lanes.engine: A broad statistical toolkit in `textstats.zig` / `textutil.zig`: PMI collocations, word/char n-grams + frequency, cosine similarity, Flesch reading-ease and grade, stopword removal, lexical diversity, and language detection.
lanes.owed: At NLTK parity for the statistical layer; mostly English-tuned (stopwords, readability). A solid, broad utility belt.

lanes.engine: `phonetics.zig` — Soundex (4-char) and Metaphone (6-char), English-oriented, pure algorithm with no data file — an extra that NLTK and spaCy don't ship.
lanes.owed: Two algorithms — no Double Metaphone, NYSIIS or Caverphone. A nice bonus over the NLP peers, short of a dedicated phonetics library.

lanes.engine: `ner.zig` — deterministic, gazetteer + POS-chunk + rules (no model): chunk NNP runs, classify via firstname / place / org gazetteers and title/context rules into PERSON / ORGANIZATION / LOCATION / ENTITY.
lanes.owed: Well below neural NER: four types, English gazetteers, no learned disambiguation. The file itself names CRF/transformer NER as "the modern-tier upgrade." The weakest classic lane against the peers.

lanes.engine: `wordnet.zig` over a compacted Princeton WordNet 3.1 (8.6 MB, ~140k words): synonyms and hypernyms, the two most-used relations, engine-backed.
lanes.owed: The compaction dropped hyponyms, meronyms, antonyms and glosses — a substantial subset of what NLTK's WordNet exposes. Synonymy and hypernymy work; the rest of the graph does not.

lanes.engine: Ring-side chunking (`Chunks("DT? JJ* NN+")`, `NounPhrases`) and a cascaded constituency parse tree (`stzParseTree`, Penn bracket notation, S→VP→PP→NP) — analogous to NLTK's `RegexpParser`.
lanes.owed: No dependency parsing — spaCy and Stanza's core capability is entirely absent, and the doc explicitly keeps it deferred. Constituency-via-cascade is the ceiling.

lanes.engine: `stzText` exposes the neural surface — `Embedding()`, `SemanticSimilarityWith()`, `Classify(labels)`, `SummarizedAbstractively()` — all gated on `HasSemanticModel()`.
lanes.owed: They no-op without a loaded GGUF model, no static word2vec/GloVe ships, and the ggml bridge + GGUF foundry that would power them is the one unstarted rung (see the Neural tier page).

gaps_title: The gaps, ordered by return — not by size
gaps_lede: Three tiers. The first unlocks the whole neural tier and lifts the weakest classic lane; the second is cheap data/coverage; the third is the deep parsing and multilingual reach.

items.title: The ggml bridge + GGUF foundry
items.text: The one unstarted rung (R4 step 8) that turns every neural delegator real — transformer NER, embeddings, abstractive summary, zero-shot classify. It rides the Neural tier page, and it is what would move this group from "beats NLTK" to "reaches spaCy."

items.title: Statistical / neural NER
items.text: A CRF or perceptron-sequence NER above the gazetteer floor — the weakest classic lane. Lifts recognition beyond four types and English name lists toward usable accuracy, without waiting on the full neural tier.

items.title: Restore the full WordNet graph
items.text: Bring back hyponyms, meronyms, antonyms and glosses that the compaction dropped — a larger data file or an on-demand loader. Closes most of the gap to NLTK's WordNet with no new algorithm.

items.title: Ship a static embedding floor
items.text: A small GloVe/word2vec embedding embedded like the other data, so `SemanticSimilarity` works without a GGUF model — the lexical-tier floor the architecture's own LAW 2 calls for.

items.title: Publish accuracy benchmarks
items.text: No POS accuracy, NER F1 or VADER-parity numbers exist — guards prove behavior, not scores. A small eval harness against standard corpora would let these ratings rest on metrics, and prove the NLTK-parity claim.

items.title: Dependency parsing
items.text: The spaCy/Stanza core, entirely absent. A transition-based parser (classic MALT-style, or on the neural tier) would add the syntactic layer that constituency-cascade only approximates.

items.title: POS-aware & multilingual lemmatization
items.text: Use POS to disambiguate lemmas, and extend beyond en/fr/ar toward the stemmer's 25-language reach — turning the dictionary lane from lookup into linguistically-correct reduction.

items.title: CJK / Thai dictionary segmentation
items.text: The tokenizer's own named future step — vendor libthai/ICU so CJK and Thai break on words, not codepoints, extending the strong tokenization lane to the scripts it currently approximates.

notes.lead: The honesty line on the ratings.
notes.text: The guards are behavioral, not benchmarked — no POS accuracy, NER F1 or VADER-parity number exists anywhere. What they prove is values and invariants: the lemmatizer's ambiguity tie-break is pinned so a data edit fails loudly, sentiment sign/ordering holds against a build-time tally over 1,000 reviews, POS/word/sentence counts agree, and multilingual input survives byte-for-byte through the English models (robustness, not linguistic correctness on non-English). So the lanes are rated on faithful-reimplementation-of-a-known-method, not on a measured score.

Softanza's NLP is the best embedded, zero-setup, deterministic classic pipeline of its peers — genuinely competitive with NLTK and simpler to reach — and a full tier below spaCy/Stanza on exactly the things that need a model: neural NER, dependency parsing and learned embeddings, all deferred to a local-model upgrade that hasn't been built yet.
